tagline: From steaming jungle to icy Patagonia
overview:
Argentina stretches down the southeastern side of South America for more than 3,500 kilometers, from tropical waterfalls in the north to glaciers and windswept islands near Antarctica. It is the eighth-largest country in the world, about 2.78 million km², roughly four times the size of Texas, with about 46 million people. Its neighbors are Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and Uruguay, and the Atlantic Ocean washes its long eastern coast.

Around a third of Argentines live in and around the capital, Buenos Aires, a huge city of grand avenues, cafes and tango halls on the Río de la Plata. Many families have Italian and Spanish roots, which shows in the food, the accents and the passion for soccer. Spanish is the national language, and Guaraní is also official in the northeastern province of Corrientes.

Argentina is a federal republic with an elected president. Farming and ranching on the vast grasslands called the Pampas have made it one of the world's great producers of beef, wheat and soybeans.
landAndNature:
The Andes form Argentina's western wall, crowned by Aconcagua, which at about 6,960 meters is the highest mountain outside Asia. East of the mountains lie the Pampas, flat, fertile grasslands that seem to run forever, and in the south the dry, windy plateau of Patagonia. In the far northeast, the Iguazú Falls thunder over 275 separate cascades on the border with Brazil.

Climate ranges from subtropical heat in the north to freezing cold in Tierra del Fuego, the island at the continent's tip. The Perito Moreno Glacier in Patagonia is famous for the towers of blue ice that crash into Lake Argentino. Wildlife includes guanacos (wild relatives of llamas), rheas, the Andean condor, Magellanic penguins, southern right whales and jaguars in the northern forests.
peopleAndCulture:
Argentines speak Spanish with a distinctive rhythm shaped by Italian immigrants, and "che" is a friendly way to get someone's attention. Life revolves around long meals: the asado, a slow barbecue of beef over wood coals, is a weekend ritual, along with empanadas, milanesas and dulce de leche, a caramel spread eaten on everything. Friends share mate, a bitter herbal tea sipped through a metal straw from a gourd.

Soccer is a national obsession, and Diego Maradona and Lionel Messi are treated as heroes after leading the team to World Cup wins in 1986 and 2022. Tango, born in the working-class ports of Buenos Aires in the late 1800s, is the country's signature music and dance. Gauchos, the horse-riding cowboys of the Pampas, remain a proud symbol of rural life.
history:
Indigenous peoples such as the Diaguita, Mapuche, Guaraní and Tehuelche lived across the land long before Spanish explorers arrived in the early 1500s. Buenos Aires was permanently founded in 1580, and the region became part of Spain's empire. On May 25, 1810, the people of Buenos Aires set up their own government, and independence was declared in 1816; General José de San Martín then led armies over the Andes to free Chile and Peru as well.

Between 1880 and 1930 millions of Europeans, especially Italians and Spaniards, arrived by ship, and Argentina became one of the richest countries on Earth. The 1900s brought political turmoil, including the popular leader Juan Perón and a military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983 in which tens of thousands of people were kidnapped and killed. After a failed war with Britain over the Falkland Islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas, democracy returned in 1983.
funFacts: The ballpoint pen was perfected and patented in Argentina in 1943 by László Bíró, a Hungarian immigrant; Argentines still call pens 'biromes.'
In 1892 Argentine police became the first in the world to solve a crime using fingerprints.
Argentinosaurus, one of the largest dinosaurs ever discovered, was found in Patagonia and may have weighed as much as ten elephants.
The country's name comes from argentum, the Latin word for silver, which early explorers hoped to find.
Ushuaia, on Tierra del Fuego, is often called the southernmost city in the world.
Buenos Aires has more bookshops per person than almost any other city on Earth.
